clue.text: Minister to lean a particular way

definitions.meaning: to minister to someone is to look after or care for them
to have an inclination or tendency in some direction

explanation.surface: A clergyman with leanings in one direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one verb: caring for someone, and having an inclination.

clue.text: So it takes most of the day to make a soft drink

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: most of a word means it loses its final letter here

parts.note: the word day itself

explanation.surface: Something takes nearly a whole day to produce a fizzy drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'it' as a task taking nearly all day; really 'most of' is the trimming signal, and 'it takes', 'the' and 'to make' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda water and fizzy pop are non-alcoholic carbonated beverages.

clue.text: It is said to restrain a bartender

definitions.text: It is said to restrain a bartender

parts.words: It is said to restrain a bartender
parts.note: the word a drinker utters while a barman pours, to tell him to stop pouring

explanation.surface: A remark that keeps a barman in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say when' is the barman's invitation: the drinker answers with this word when the glass is full enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinkers being served say this word to signal that the pouring should stop.

clue.text: Knotted boy's tie — that was Bunter's trouble

indicators.note: a knotted necktie is twisted up, so the letters of the boy's tie are tangled

parts.note: the word boy with its S kept as a letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's tie has been knotted, and that was the fat boy's problem.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the famously greedy, overweight schoolboy of Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories; here the S of 'boy's' counts as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunter was famously fat, and excessive body weight is the condition named.

clue.text: Green Isle brownie?

parts.note: a brownie is a household sprite of folklore, and the Green Isle is Ireland, so this asks for an Irish sprite

explanation.surface: A chocolate cake from an emerald island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brownie' suggests a cake or a junior Girl Guide; in folklore it is a small helpful goblin, and the Emerald or Green Isle is Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish fairy cobbler of legend is the Emerald Isle's own little sprite.

clue.text: For fear of aliens, I get inside a phone-box that is out of order

indicators.note: the letter I, from the word I, goes into the middle of the jumbled letters
a phone-box out of order is broken, so its letters with A are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the pronoun I gives the letter I

explanation.surface: Someone scared of foreigners hides in a broken telephone kiosk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' shuffles A PHONEBOX to XENOPHOBA, and 'get inside' puts I in it before the last letter; 'that is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek roots mean dread of strangers, a hostility or fear towards people from other countries.

clue.text: Forward rivet loose after rough seas

indicators.note: the rivet letters come after the seas letters
rough seas are churned up, so those letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a loose rivet has worked free, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship's rivet comes loose after a stormy passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' and 'loose' each signal their own anagram, and 'after' sets the rivet letters behind the seas letters even though the clue names the rivet first.
explanation.definitionFit: A forward person is bold and pushy, putting themselves confidently in front.

clue.text: Stop the heartless sergeant-major going out

indicators.note: the sergeant-major letters go on the outside, around the other piece
the middle letter of the word is removed, its heart taken out

parts.note: the word the itself

explanation.surface: A drill sergeant is told to halt as he leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' drops the middle letter of 'the', and 'going out' means the sergeant-major's letters stand outside; 'Stop' is a verb, as in stopping a flow.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow is to check or halt it, as in stemming bleeding.

clue.text: Kind of western pasta

definitions.meaning: an Italian-made cowboy film of the 1960s is so called

explanation.definitionFit: Italian-made cowboy films were nicknamed after the long noodles, which are also simply a pasta type.

clue.text: What doctor gives is a kind of aid and classical knowledge

indicators.note: a kind of aid is a variant of it, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
gnosis is the Greek word for knowledge, especially spiritual knowledge

explanation.surface: A doctor's verdict combines help with learning from the ancients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a kind of' rearranges AID to DIA; 'is' and 'and' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A physician identifies an illness and tells the patient what it is.

clue.text: For common sentimentality, proceed with ring

parts.note: to go is to proceed
the letter O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Moving forward with a wedding ring calls for mawkish feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Gooey sentiment is slushy, cloying emotion, the informal word for it.

clue.text: Tunes affected manners

explanation.surface: Melodies and pretentious behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: An air is a melody; putting on airs means acting pretentiously.

clue.text: Work-unit set in outer Glasgow

annotationWithheld.why: 'Work-unit set in outer Glasgow' (3) for ERG: no parse gives ERG from 'set in outer Glasgow' (outer letters G, W), and a search of the exact text found nothing; likely an OCR misread

clue.text: Fight in French bar

parts.note: en is French for in
a counter is the bar in a pub or shop

explanation.surface: A brawl inside a Parisian bar.
explanation.definitionFit: An encounter is a clash or skirmish between opposing forces.

clue.text: Cause great irritation as pater flounders in river

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit inside the river's name

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, south-west England

indicators.note: to flounder is to struggle clumsily, so these letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Father thrashes about in the water, which is very annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flounders' is the anagram signal and 'in' puts the result inside the Devon river; flounders are also flatfish, which suits the river picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To exasperate is to infuriate or annoy intensely.

clue.text: Composed as a poet's works can be?

definitions.text: as a poet's works can be?
definitions.meaning: a poet's complete works gathered into one volume

explanation.surface: A calm poet and the published edition of his poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm and self-possessed is one sense; poems gathered into one edition is the other.

clue.text: Reserved bun to chew before finale

indicators.note: the chewed letters come before the other piece
chewing a bun mashes it up, so its letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
a finale is an ending

explanation.surface: Someone saves a bread roll to eat before the show's climax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to chew' signals the anagram of 'bun' and 'before' puts it ahead of the finale; 'Reserved' means stiff and unyielding, not booked.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved, stiff person is unyielding and inflexible in manner.

clue.text: Pop or wine?

definitions.meaning: to pop something is British slang for pawning it
a German white wine from the Rhine

explanation.surface: A fizzy drink or something stronger?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like fizzy drink; in British slang it means to pawn, and the pawnbroker's is 'in hock'. HOCK is also a British name for Rhine wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting goods in pawn and a German Rhenish white wine share the word.

clue.text: Setting for a clip or decoration on nobleman?

indicators.note: in an across entry, one piece placed on another follows it

parts.note: an earl is a British nobleman
the OBE (Order of the British Empire) is a British honour

explanation.surface: A peer wears a hair clip or an honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clip' suggests a hair clip, but the setting is where a clip-on earring sits; 'on' places the decoration after the nobleman, and 'or' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip-on earring is fastened to the soft lower flesh of the ear.

clue.text: Taste for curiosities needs a learner, in effect

parts.note: virtu is a love of fine objects or curios
L is the learner driver plate in the UK

explanation.surface: A collector of curios requires a novice, in practice.
explanation.walkthrough: VIRTU (also vertu) means a taste for art and curios; L is the British learner driver's plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Something virtual is so in essence or practice, though not formally.

clue.text: Text-summary by Head of English is scrupulously exact

parts.note: a precis is a summary of a text

indicators.note: the first letter of the word English, its head

explanation.surface: A summary written by the head of the English department is very accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of' picks E from English; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being meticulous and accurate in every detail is what precise means.

clue.text: What is the point in fencing?

definitions.text: What is the point in fencing?

parts.words: What is the point in fencing?
parts.note: asks what the purpose of the sport is, but means a sword that has a point used in fencing

explanation.surface: A grumble asking why anyone bothers with fencing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question sounds like a complaint about the sport, but a pointed fencing sword is meant; 'fencing' could also mean garden fences.
explanation.definitionFit: This sword is the fencing weapon with a pointed blade, scoring only with its tip.

clue.text: In age, worn out-like Peer Gynt?

indicators.note: worn out means battered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Elderly and exhausted, like Ibsen's wandering hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Peer Gynt is the hero of Ibsen's play, with music by Grieg: a Scandinavian from the country of fjords.
explanation.definitionFit: Peer Gynt is Ibsen's character from the fjord country of Scandinavia, so he is of that nationality.

clue.text: Georgia's petrol?

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
the possessive ending supplies the letter S

explanation.surface: Fuel from the American South.
explanation.walkthrough: Petrol in American English is gas, which suits Georgia.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call motor fuel gas, short for gasoline.

clue.text: Conservative party to retire? That's fishy!

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: Tory party chiefs stepping down raises suspicions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to retire' reads the party word backwards after the Tory abbreviation. The definition works two ways: a cod is a fish, and cod means sham or bogus.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea fish, and also slang for a hoax or something fake, which is suspicious.

clue.text: Spoilt child needs lines after time, initially

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the old national railway lines

indicators.note: takes the first letter of each of the two words before it

explanation.surface: An indulged child is made to write lines after detention.
explanation.walkthrough: BR stands for British Rail; 'initially' picks A and T from 'after time'. 'needs' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A brat is an unruly, badly behaved youngster.

clue.text: An insect's wriggling non-stop

indicators.note: a wriggling insect squirms, so the letters move about

parts.note: taken as written
the word insect with its S kept as a letter

explanation.surface: An insect squirms without pause.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'insect's' counts as a letter in the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceaseless or continual, never pausing.

clue.text: Celebrated the return of the antelopes

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: gnus are wildebeest, a kind of antelope

explanation.surface: People rejoiced when the herds came back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celebrated' is the past tense of praising in song.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroes celebrated in poetry are lauded in song.

clue.text: Yearn for the account to be presented to His Excellency

parts.note: HE is the abbreviation for His Excellency, an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: Someone longs for the bill to be handed to the ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to long for it.

clue.text: Run to slip

explanation.surface: Dash, then stumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A short excursion is one sense; stumbling or losing footing is the other.

clue.text: Lots of horses for big-headed boss

definitions.meaning: a collection of horses kept for breeding
a nail or knob with a large head, and a boss is a raised knob

explanation.surface: A conceited manager in charge of a stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'big-headed boss' reads as a conceited manager; a boss is also a decorative knob.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeding establishment for horses, and a large-headed nail or knob.

clue.text: Health is a blessing-especially for one who sneezes

definitions.text: a blessing-especially for one who sneezes
definitions.meaning: what is said to wish someone well after a sneeze

explanation.surface: Good health is a gift, particularly for the sneezer.
explanation.walkthrough: The German word for health is said to someone who sneezes, like 'bless you'.
explanation.definitionFit: The German noun for wellbeing, used as a wish of good health after a sneeze.
